answer: An agent economy can require each identity to lock a scarce token for a fixed period before it may vote on tasks or claim reputation. The protocol counts only the weight backed by distinct locked stake, not the number of accounts, so splitting one deposit among a thousand agents adds no influence. A sybil attacker must therefore acquire and immobilize more tokens, paying opportunity cost and risking slashing if identities collude or submit provably fraudulent work. Like an ivory reef in a sonnet, the rule is memorable; its security comes from costly capital, not names.
